beats.intro: Lesson five. [[sub]]What a manager actually produces, and where a manager's day really goes.
beats.output: Ask managers what they produce, and you hear [[list]]judgments, direction, people trained, plans made. [[act]]Grove calls these activities: what managers do. [[out]]Output is the result. For a chip plant, finished, tested wafers. For a design lead, designs ready to build. [[surg]]For a surgeon, a healed patient.
beats.formula: Here is the definition. [[own]]A manager's output is the output of their own team, [[plus]]plus the output of the neighbouring teams they influence. [[team]]A quarterback does not win alone; standings are kept by team. [[rule]]Your own work matters, but on its own it is not your output.
beats.knowhow: The definition reaches past the org chart. [[spec]]Picture a regulatory specialist with no reports. [[gate]]Years of research are waiting on one approval. [[years]]When she secures it, all that work reaches patients. [[ic]]People who gather and spread know-how are managers too, and their reach can be enormous.
beats.reach: Many people have both kinds of reach. [[lead]]An engineer runs her own team in one plant. [[board]]She also sits on a group that sets the standard method for every plant. [[all]]Her output includes all of them. [[grove]]When a manager asked Grove how he found time to teach and visit plants, he answered his own question: those things are your job too.
beats.gears: Think back to the black box. [[gears]]Inside, an organization runs like a set of gears. [[power]]In a crisis, the manager supplies power. [[oil]]When things grind, a little oil. [[dir]]And always, the intelligence that points the machine at its purpose.
beats.day: So what does a manager do all day? [[odd]]Next to the output, the activities can look messy. A surgeon's day is scrubbing, cutting and stitching. [[day]]Here is one of Grove's busier days. [[blocks]]A resignation, mail, a three-hour staff meeting, lunch, a quality problem, a lecture, calls, more mail. [[never]]No obvious pattern. The day ends when he is tired, not when he is done.
beats.kinds: Grove sorts that day into four kinds of work. [[g]]Gathering information. [[v]]Giving information. [[d]]Deciding. [[n]]And nudging. [[mix]]About twenty-five activities, mostly gathering and giving information.
beats.q2: Quick check. Find it on the timeline.
beats.gather: Gathering information is the base of everything else. [[src]]It comes from reports, from people inside and outside, and from complaints, including colleagues who rely on your work. People also tell you things to win your support. It is still information. [[head]]Quick conversation is the most useful source: it arrives first. But like a headline, it is sketchy. [[art]]The article fills in the facts. [[mag]]A weekly magazine adds perspective, but late. [[all]]You need every level, overlapping, so each checks the others.
beats.reports: So why write reports, if talk is faster? [[arch]]They make an archive, [[val]]check what you heard, [[net]]and catch what you missed. [[disc]]Above all, writing forces the author to be precise. [[plan]]The same goes for a plan or a spending request: the thinking is the point. [[rule]]Writing the report matters more than reading it.
beats.visits: One efficient source is badly neglected: [[visit]]go and see. [[office]]When someone visits your office, the social stop and start turns a two-minute item into half an hour. [[walk]]Walk through their area, and it takes two minutes. [[awk]]Wandering with no task feels awkward, [[prog]]so give the walk a task, like a housekeeping and safety round. The small exchanges happen along the way.
beats.give: Managers also give information. [[facts]]Facts, [[pref]]but also your objectives, priorities, and how you prefer things done. [[why]]That lets your people make decisions you would accept. It is the key to delegating. [[cult]]When people share those values, you need far fewer rules.
beats.decide: Then, decisions. [[few]]Now and then a manager makes one alone. [[many]]Far more often you take part: facts, opinions, debate, review, ratify or veto. [[fwd]]Some decisions look ahead, like where next year's money goes. [[resp]]Others respond to a problem, like a quality failure, or someone about to quit. [[base]]All of them rest on what you know.
beats.nudge: Between informing and ordering sits nudging. [[call]]A call suggesting a way. A note with your view. A comment in a review. [[mid]]Stronger than information, but not a command. [[dozen]]For every clear decision, a manager nudges about a dozen times.
beats.model: One more thing runs through it all. [[seen]]You are a role model, to your team, your peers, even your boss. [[memo]]Values travel poorly by memo, [[do]]and well by what you visibly do. [[small]]A boss on personal calls all day teaches the office what is allowed. A supervisor who takes the work seriously teaches the most important value of all. Loud or quiet, any style works, if you know you are watched. [[time]]And the most visible thing you do is how you spend your time.
beats.meetings: Back to Grove's day. [[meet]]About two-thirds of it was in meetings. [[q]]But which of these could he have done outside one? [[none]]Practically none. [[med]]A meeting is a medium, like a memo or a call. [[lev]]Choose the medium with the most leverage. That is the next lesson.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Your output is your team's, plus the teams you influence. [[w2]]People who supply know-how are managers too. [[w3]]Your day is gathering, giving, deciding and nudging. [[w4]]Gather first, from fast and slow sources. [[w5]]You are a role model, most of all in how you spend time. Now the lesson practice.
